To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the richness, abundance, community structure and composition of leaf-litter amphibians and reptile communities in three mono-dominant native tree species plantations were significantly different than those in nearby primary forest in northeastern Costa Rica.
mono-dominant tree species plantations support a diverse community of frogs and litters, and some species support more diverse communities of frogs and lizzards than primary forest.
mono-dominant tree plantations of Pentaclethra macrolova, Vochysie guatemalensis, and Virola koschyni support different herpetofaunas from each other and from nearby primary forest.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of habitat fragmentation and forest conversion on the herpetofaunas of tropical rainforests, and how these changes may influence the structure and function of these communities.

how the species richness, community composition, and abundance of amphibians and lizards in the leaf-litter of tropical forests is affected by human land-use change and habitat fragmentation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mono-dominant plantation species can facilitate the restoration or maintenance of native herpetofaunas on degraded landscapes.

our results indicate that the species richness and abundance of herpetofaunas in mono-dominance plantations of three different species is not as rich and abundant as in primary forest, however, they can support a different assemblages and richness of frogs and lizards than primary forest.

the herpetofaunas of these plantations are not as rich as the primary forest, but that they do have a high degree of similarity to the primary forest, and that they can serve as a refuge for herpetofaunals that would otherwise be absent from the plantation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the species richness of amphibians and lizards is greater in primary forest than in mono-dominance tree plantations, and that community composition is different among tree species.
mono-dominant tree plantations can support amphibian and reptile assemblages that are similar to those of primary forest in species richness and community assembly.
the species composition of the herpetofaunae in these plantations is similar to the species composition of herpetofaunas in primary forests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conservation of biodiversity can be achieved through a mosaic of primary forest and plantation habitats.

mono-dominant tree plantations can provide habitat for herpetofaunas and that the species of trees planted in plantations can affect the composition and structure of the herpetofaunate communities that they support.
mono-specific plantation forests can be a viable option in the short term, but the long-term success of these plantations is uncertain.
